parts.title: Let’s teach them how to teach
parts.subtitle: What matters in schools is teaching. Fortunately, teaching can be taught
parts.article:
Let’s teach them how to teach

(A) Forget smart uniforms and small classes. The secret to stellar grades and thriving students is teachers. One US study found that in a single year’s teaching the top 10% of teachers impart three times as much learning to their pupils as the worst 10% do. Another US study suggests that if black pupils were taught by the best quarter of teachers, the gap between their achievement and that of white pupils would disappear. But efforts to ensure that every teacher can teach are hindered by the persistent myth that good teachers are born, not made. Government policies, which often start from the same assumption, seek to raise teaching standards by attracting high flying graduates to join the profession and prodding bad teachers to leave. Teachers’ unions, meanwhile, insist that if only their members were free from centralised policies, excellence would follow.

(B) The premise that teaching ability is something you either have or don’t is mistaken. A new breed of teacher trainers is founding a rigorous science of pedagogy. The aim is to make ordinary teachers great, just as sports coaches help athletes of all abilities to improve their personal best. Done right, this will revolutionise schools and change lives.

(C) Education has a history of lurching from one ‘miracle’ solution to the next. The best of them even achieve some good. The US initiative Teach for America has brought energetic new graduates into the profession, and dismissing teachers for bad performance has boosted results in Washington, DC. But each approach has its limits. Teaching is a mass profession: it cannot grab all the top graduates, year after year. When poor teachers are fired, new ones are needed – and they will have come through the same educational system that failed to make fine teachers of their predecessors.

(D) By contrast, the idea of improving the average teacher could revolutionise the entire profession. Around the world, few newly qualified teachers are well enough prepared for the classroom. A recent report found 31 countries in which more than a quarter of primary-school teachers had not reached minimal national standards. In rich countries, the problem is subtler. Teachers qualify after completing a long, specialised course, which almost always involves superficial and seemingly useless discussions of theory. Some of these courses, including master’s degrees in education, have no effect on how well their graduates’ pupils end up being taught.

(E) What teachers fail to learn in universities and teacher-training colleges they rarely pick up on the job. They become better teachers in their first few years as they get to grips with real pupils in real classrooms, but after that improvements tail off. This is largely because schools neglect their most important learners: teachers themselves. Across the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) club of mostly rich countries, two-fifths of teachers say they have never had a chance to learn by sitting in on another teacher’s lessons; nor have they been asked to give feedback on their peers.

(F) If this is to change, teachers need to learn how to impart knowledge and prepare young minds to receive and retain it. Good teachers set clear goals, enforce high standards of behaviour and manage their lesson time wisely. They use tried-and-tested instructional techniques to ensure that all brains are working all the time – for example, asking questions in the classroom with “cold calling*” rather than relying on the same eager pupils putting up their hands.

(G) Like other complex skills, teaching requires a route to mastery that is not based on abstruse theory but on intense, guided practice grounded in subject-matter knowledge and pedagogical methods. Trainees should spend more time in the classroom. The places where pupils do best – for example, Finland, Singapore and Shanghai – put novice teachers through a demanding apprenticeship. In the US, high-performing schools teach trainees in the classroom and bring them on with coaching and feedback.

(H) Teacher-training institutions need to be more rigorous. A century ago, medical schools raised the calibre of doctors by introducing systematic curriculums and providing clinical experience. It is essential that teacher-training colleges start to collect and publish data on how their graduates perform in the classroom. Courses that produce teachers who go on to do little to improve their pupils’ learning should not receive subsidies or see their graduates become teachers. They would then have to improve to survive.

(I) Big changes are needed in schools, too, to ensure that teachers improve throughout their careers. Teachers in the best ones hone their craft through observation and coaching. They accept critical feedback, which their unions should not resist but welcome, as it is only proper for people doing such an important job. The best head teachers hold novices’ hands by helping them prepare high quality lessons and arranging for more-experienced teachers to cover for them when they need time for further study and practice.

(J) Money is less important than one might think. Teachers in top-of-the-class Finland, for example, earn about the OECD average. But ensuring the best teachers stay in the classroom will, in most places, mean paying more. People who thrive in front of pupils should not have to become managers to earn a pay rise. And more flexibility on salaries would make it much easier to attract the best teachers to the worst schools.

(K) Improving the quality of the average teacher would raise the profession’s prestige, setting up a virtuous cycle in which more talented graduates clamoured to join. But the biggest gains will come from preparing new teachers better, and upgrading the ones already in classrooms.

questions.question: The author suggests that head teachers can assist newly qualified teachers by

analyses.content: 原文说最好的校长会“牵着新手的手（hold novices’ hands）”手把手帮他们备课，这就意味着校长需要在实际工作中与新老师紧密合作。
你可能看到前面有一句“observation and coaching”就想选A（亲自做课堂观察），但那是优秀学校里老师们互相磨练技艺的方式，校长真正给新手的直接支持是带他们备课和排班。

I段：The best head teachers hold novices’ hands by helping them prepare high quality lessons and arranging for more-experienced teachers to cover for them when they need time for further study and practice.

analyses.content: 原文直接批评了师范培训中对理论的探讨是“肤浅且似乎无用的”，并且明确指出教学不应基于深奥的理论，这与题干称“理论是必不可少的一部分”完全相反。
你可能会因为自身常识觉得理论知识很重要而错选YES，但做判断题必须严格根据原文作者的立场来，作者在这篇文章里是强烈“反纯理论、重实践”的。

analyses.content: 原文只提到了“钱没有大家想的那么重要”，以及在某些地方需要给优秀老师涨薪的问题，但完全没有探讨当前整个教育体系“是否经费不足（underfunded）”以及“经费不足是否导致了学校问题”。
你可能会看到最后一段讲需要提高薪水以留住好老师，就自行脑补“原来是因为教育资金不足惹的祸”，切忌在雅思阅读里做这种跨步推理。

questions.question: Good classroom teachers should be paid more to remain in the classroom.

analyses.content: 原文直接表明，为了确保最优秀的老师留在教室里继续教书，在大多数地方都意味着“要付给他们更多薪水（paying more）”，不能逼着好老师去当管理层才能加薪。
你可能会因为段首有一句“钱没那么重要”而犹豫不敢选，但紧接着作者就用“But”转折，明确提出了必须用更高的薪水来把好老师留在课堂上的具体主张。
J段：But ensuring the best teachers stay in the classroom will, in most places, mean paying more. People who thrive in front of pupils should not have to become managers to earn a pay rise.

questions.question: Just as any athlete can be coached for better performance,

analyses.content: B段：The aim is to make ordinary teachers great, just as sports coaches help athletes of all abilities to improve their personal best.
原文把“教练帮助各种能力的运动员刷新个人最好成绩”和“让普通老师变得优秀”放在了一起做类比，所以运动员能提高对应着“不突出的老师也能被改善”。
你可能想直接去选项里找“sports”或者“coach”的对应词，但匹配题考察的是句子前后的逻辑对应对象，即运动员（athlete）对应的是普通的老师（ordinary teachers）。

questions.question: If teachers are to be taught the complex skills they require,

analyses.content: 原文指出掌握教学这项复杂技能的途径，不是基于深奥的理论，而是基于密集且有指导的“实践（practice）”，直接说明了实践远比理论重要。
你可能会被F选项（更好的大纲和更多实践）迷惑，但这道题句子里强调的核心对比是“not based on theory but on practice”，选项A极其精准地概括了这层对比关系。
G段：Like other complex skills, teaching requires a route to mastery that is not based on abstruse theory but on intense, guided practice grounded in subject-matter knowledge and pedagogical methods.

questions.question: In teaching, as in the medical profession,

analyses.content: 文中提到医学院当年通过引入系统的课程（对应syllabus）和提供临床经验（对应practical involvement）提高了医生水准，要求师范学院也照做，完美对应了F选项。
你可能通读了选项觉得好几个都说得通，但题目明确给出了“medical profession”的定位词，只要对照原文找出医学院的具体做法，就能立刻锁定F选项。
H段：A century ago, medical schools raised the calibre of doctors by introducing systematic curriculums and providing clinical experience. It is essential that teacher-training colleges start to...

questions.question: If the status of teachers were improved,

analyses.content: 原文结尾处明示，提高普通老师的质量能提升这个职业的声望（即题干中的status），从而形成良性循环，吸引“更多有才华的毕业生（more talented graduates）”加入。
你可能会觉得最后一段的句子很长看不太懂，但只要牢牢抓住“more talented graduates”，对应到C选项的“more capable graduates”，就能轻松拿下这道压轴题。
K段：Improving the quality of the average teacher would raise the profession’s prestige, setting up a virtuous cycle in which more talented graduates clamoured to join.
